IN SUPPORT OF RESPONDENTS
_________________________
INTEREST S OF AMICI CURIAE 1
The questions before this Court are whether the
National Voter Registration Act of 1993 (“NVRA”) prohibits Arizona from (1) requiring voter-registration applicants to produce “satisfactory” documentary evidence of
U.S. citizenship when registering with a S tate registration form and (2) implementing a systematic program
within 90 days of a Federal election to cancel the registrations of voters who are alleged to be noncitizens. The
answers to both questions implicate not just the plain text
of the NVRA but also the very purposes for which it was
enacted three decades ago—thus requiring a clear understanding of why and how Congress struck a balance

1  Pursuant to this Court’s Rule 37.6, counsel for Amici state that
no party or counsel for a party, or any other person other than Amici
and their counsel, made a monetary contribution to fund the preparation or submission of this brief.

2

between expanding the registration of eligible electors
and ensuring the integrity and accuracy of voter rolls.
Amici are current and former  members of Congress
who worked on and helped pass the NVRA:
David Bonior
Democratic Representative from Michigan,
1977–2003
Maria Cantwell
Democratic Representative from Washington,
1993–1995;
Democratic Senator from Washington,
2001–present
James Clyburn
Democratic Representative from South Carolina,
1993–present
Anthony Coelho
Democratic Representative from California,
1979–1989
Richard Gephardt
Democratic Representative from Missouri,
1977–2005
Steny Hoyer
Democratic Representative from Maryland,
1981–present
Jay Inslee
Democratic Representative from Washington,
1993–1995, 1999–2012
Jerrold Nadler
Democratic Representative from New York,
1992–present

3

Eleanor Holmes Norton,
Democratic Delegate from the District of
Columbia,
1991–present
Nancy Pelosi
Democratic Representative from California,
1987–present
James Walsh,
Republican Representative from New York,
1989–2009
Maxine Waters,
Democratic Representative from California,
1991–present
Ronald Wyden,
Democratic Representative from Oregon,
1981–1996;
Democratic Senator from Oregon,
1996–present
Representatives Coelho and Walsh served on the House
Administration Subcommittee on Elections that considered the initial version of the NVRA at the time it was
drafted during the 101st Congress. Representative Hoyer
was a member of that same subcommittee during the
103rd Congress and was also a conferee on the committee
that reconciled the House and Senate versions of the
NVRA. Representatives Bonior, Cantwell, Gephardt,
Hoyer, and Inslee were original cosponsors of the NVRA
and were ultimately joined as cosponsors by Representatives Clyburn, Nadler, and Pelosi and Delegate Norton .
Representatives Gephardt and Bonior served in the
Democratic House leadership and helped guide the
NVRA to enactment during the 103rd Congress. And  all
Amici who served in Congress at the time of the NVRA’s
passage voted in favor of the legislation,  and Delegate

4

Norton supported its passage, based on their understandings of its intended purposes and effects.
Amici submit this brief to provide their unique perspective on Congress’s goals in enacting the NVRA. See,
e.g., Hewitt v. United States, 606 U.S. 419, 425 (2025)
(citing amicus brief from lead Senate sponsors of statute
at issue); United States v. Cooley, 593 U.S. 345, 355 (2021)
(citing amicus briefs by current and former members of
Congress regarding legislative intent).
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The NVRA carefully balances multiple key considerations. See 52 U.S.C. § 20501(a) –(b) (enumerating Congress’s findings and NVRA’s purposes). Congress sought
to increase the registration of eligible voters by making
the process easier and more accessible through clear and
uniform standards for F ederal elections. At the same
time, Congress recognized the need to maintain standards
and practices to protect election integrity and ensure current and accurate voter rolls . These goals were informed
by real-world examples of practical challenges and solutions that had worked well in States  that had adopted
them.
As members of Congress who  worked on, supported,
and helped pass the NVRA, A mici are keenly aware of
these complex considerations and offer two points to
inform this Court’s resolution of this case.
First, the NVRA generally prohibits systematic voterroll maintenance and purges during the 90 days preceding
a Federal election (the “90-Day Quiet Period”), which was
intended to provide broad protection for voters who might
be swept up erroneously in last -minute list maintenance
and risk disenfranchisement. Congress understood at the
time of the NVRA’s enactment that altering voter rolls

5

close to an election c ould cause chaos, confusion, and
unwarranted difficulties for voters and election officials
alike. At the same time, Congress recognized the
importance of accurate and up -to-date voter rolls to
ensure election integrity and public confidence. Balancing
these considerations, the NVRA broadly allows States to
conduct systematic voter -roll maintenance throughout
the year—but not during the 90-Day Quiet Period, when
correcting mistakes might no longer be feasible. Because
Arizona’s challenged law allows systematic removal of
voters during the 90 -Day Quiet Period based on citizenship—a category of removal that falls outside Congress’s
specifically enumerated and carefully crafted  exceptions—it cannot stand.
Second, Arizona’s challenged documentary proof of
citizenship (“DPOC”) regime  violates both the text and
spirit of the NVRA, thwarting the law’s objective of making voter registration more uniform and accessible and
imposing additional requirements on voters to register for
Federal elections that go beyond the limits of  the statutory text.
ARGUMENT
Congress crafted the NVRA against the backdrop of
record-low rates of voter participation in the United
States. Amici recognized that Congress could not address
every reason for low voter turnout but could at least
implement clear, uniform standards to make registering
to vote in Federal elections easier and more accessible. In
considering the initial version of the NVRA in 1989, Representative Al Swift, the chair of the House Administration Subcommittee on Elections, explained that,
[w]hile it is not in the power of this subcommittee
to motivate people to vote, it is in the power of the
subcommittee to propose legislation which makes

6

the participation process as accessible and secure
as possible. It has been made abundantly clear that
present registration procedures, as varied as they
are in each of the 50 States, have created a sufficient impediment to the voting process to warrant
a Federal response.
Voter Registration: Hearing Before the Subcomm. on
Elections of the H. Comm. on H. Admin., 101st Cong. 39
(1989) (“NVRA Hearing”).
Along with this overarching goal of increasing voter
registration and participation, Congress also recognized
the importance of keeping voter rolls accurate and current. These purposes are all clearly laid out in the statutory text:
(1) to establish procedures that will increase the
number of eligible citizens who register to vote in
elections for Federal office;
(2) to make it possible for Federal, State, and local
governments to implement this chapter in a manner that enhances the participation of eligible citizens as voters in elections for Federal office;
(3) to protect the integrity of the electoral process;
and
(4) to ensure that accurate and current voter registration rolls are maintained.
52 U.S.C. § 20501(b).
To effectively vindicate these considerations, the
enacted version of the NVRA benefited from considerable
testimony about barriers to voter registration and what
worked in practice to address them. Among the real-world
feedback Congress received—and directly relevant to the
issues before this Court—were warnings against late -
stage purges and recommendations for keeping

7

registration applications simple to enable the success of
largescale voter-registration drives.
A. Congress mandated the 90-Day Quiet Period to guard
against disenfranchisement and confusion in the
immediate lead-up to Federal elections.
Congress intended the 90 -Day Quiet Period  to be
broadly implemented and ensure that eligible voters are
not mistakenly removed from the rolls at the last minute
based on flawed data or methodology. In crafting this provision, Congress balanced the law’s key objective of
increasing eligible voter registrations with the need to
safeguard election integrity, resulting in a compromise
that allows for individualized removals within 90 days of
Federal elections while preventing the indiscriminate
application of systematic sweeps.
1. Last-minute systematic list maintenance results in
high-stakes errors and hardship for both voters and
election administrators.
The 90-Day Quiet Period requires that “[a] State shall
complete, not later than 90 days prior to the date of a primary or general election for Federal office, any program
the purpose of which is to systematically remove the
names of ineligible voters from the official lists of eligible
voters.” 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(A).
Amici understood that the 90 -Day Quiet Period was
meant to provide expansive protection given the inevitable errors that occur during systematic list maintenance.
The text reflects this intended scope : “[A]ny” systematic
program must be completed before the 90 -Day Quiet
Period, and Congress referred to removal of “ ineligible
voters” broadly, not a limited  subset of ineligible voters
(such as those who later became ineligible after initially
registering). Simply put,  all systematic list-maintenance
programs must cease during the 90 days prior to a

8

Federal election  other than a few carefully considered
exceptions enumerated in the statute. See infra pp. 10–11.
The expansiveness of the 90-Day Quiet Period effectuates Congress’s goal of protecting eligible voters from
mistaken removal shortly before elections, when such
errors are most likely to lead to disenfranchisement. As
the Eleventh Circuit has explained,
[a]t most times during the election cycle, the benefits of systematic programs outweigh the costs
because eligible voters who are incorrectly
removed have enough time to rectify any errors. In
the final days before an election, however, the
calculus changes. Eligible voters removed days or
weeks before Election Day will likely not be able to
correct the State’s errors in time to vote.
Arcia v. Fla. Sec’y of State, 772 F.3d 1335, 1346 (11th Cir.
2014). Congress expressly recognized in the NVRA that
“the right of citizens of the United States to vote is a fundamental right,” 52 U.S.C. § 20501(a)(1)—and the 90-Day
Quiet Period provides indispensable protection for that
fundamental right.
It is not just voters who benefit from the NVRA’s mandated forbearance. “ [R]unning a statewide election is a
complicated endeavor…. [T]housands of state and local
officials and volunteers must participate in a massive
coordinated effort to implement the lawmakers’ policy
choices on the ground before and during the election, and
again in counting the votes afterwards.” Democratic Nat’l
Comm. v. Wis. State Legislature , 592 U.S. 1039, 1043
(2020) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring). Last -minute list
maintenance of a systematic nature—and the challenge of
addressing the inevitable mistakes that result from such
list maintenance in a compressed timeframe—would only

9

add to the considerable stresses of election administration.
Congress crafted the NVRA with these pragmatic
concerns in mind, drawing on the experiences of States
that had already implemented various voter -registration
policies and strategies. In particular, the NVRA’s drafters relied heavily on the practical expert ise of election
administrators and other experts. D uring the initial consideration of the NVRA, the National Association of Secretaries of State (“NASS”) —a nonpartisan organization
intimately familiar with the challenges faced by S tate
election administrators—submitted a particularly impactful report titled “Barriers to Voting .” NVRA Hearing ,
supra, at 54–78. The NASS report recommended that
[a]ll purging should be done as soon as practicable
after November general elections, so registrants
will have time to return reply cards to maintain
registration for the next election cycle. Purges
should never be conducted immediately before an
election.
Id. at 73 (emphasis added).
Congress heeded NASS’s expert guidance. The
NVRA requires States to “conduct a general program
that makes a reasonable effort to remove” certain ineligible voters from the rolls , 52 U.S.C. § 20507(a)(4) , thus
ensuring accuracy and accountability.  But, as NASS
wisely urged, the NVRA limits the timing  of systematic
programs, mandating that they be completed no later
than 90 days prior to a F ederal election, see id.
§ 20507(c)(2)(A)—at which point an eligible voter mistakenly removed from the voter rolls would likely be unable
to correct the error in time to cast a ballot. The NVRA
thus expects States to conduct widespread list maintenance during the months before  the 90-Day Quiet Period

10

begins but restricts their ability to do so when the consequences of erroneous removal would be most insurmountable for innocent voters. As the Eleventh Circuit put it,
“[t]his is why the 90  Day Provision strikes a careful balance: It permits systematic removal programs at any time
except for the 90 days before an election because that is
when the risk of disenfranchising eligible voters is the
greatest.” Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1346.
Notably, the 90-Day Quiet Period was uncontroversial
at the time of the NVRA’s passage . To illustrate, w hile
opponents of the bill  proposed several amendments during the House  Administration Committee’s  mark-up,
none attempted to abolish or even narrow the limitation
on purging voter rolls within 90 days of a Federal election.
See H.R. Rep. No. 103 -9, at 36–37 (1993). All these committee members, regardless of partisan affiliation, recognized the merits of a broad ban on eleventh-hour purges.
2. Arizona’s challenged law does not qualify for
Congress’s limited exceptions to the 90-Day Quiet
Period.
“Where Congress explicitly enumerates certain
exceptions to a general prohibition, additional exceptions
are not to be implied, in the absence of evidence of a contrary legislative intent.” Andrus v. Glover Constr. Co., 446
U.S. 608, 616–17 (1980); accord  TRW Inc. v. Andrews,
534 U.S. 19, 28 (2001) (“ Expressio unius est exclusion
alterius.” ( citation modified)). Congress’s limited exceptions to the NVRA’s 90 -Day Quiet Period were specific
and carefully considered. These include allowing removals
“at the request of the registrant ,” “by reason of criminal
conviction or mental incapacity,” or due to the registrant’s
death. 52 U.S.C. § 20507(a)(3)–(4). The NVRA also allows
for “correction of registration records pursuant to this
chapter.” Id. § 20507(c)(2)(B)(ii). But that’s it—the NVRA

11

does not contemplate additional grounds for removal
apart from its enumerated exceptions.
Significantly, each of these exceptions helps mitigate
at least some concerns regarding large scale errors and
removals. Action “at the request of the registrant,” for
example, does not present a risk of mistaken removal ,
considering that the  registrant themsel f makes the
request to election officials. Congress further determined
that removals by reason of criminal conviction, mental
incapacity, or death would not present excessive  risks of
mistaken removal because information about th ese contingencies comes from other agencies that regularly provide such information to State officials. These r emovals
are also more targeted and thus better suited for an individualized and vetted inquiry within a short timeframe. 2
Moreover—and again reflecting the NVRA’s emphasis on
pragmatic solutions—Congress understood that the numbers of affected individuals in the limited categories of
criminal conviction, death, and mental incapacity would be
smaller in practice than in other potential categories, further reducing the chance of mistaken removal.
In stark contrast, removals based on citizenship raise
distinct concerns. Systematic efforts typically involve the

2  To illustrate, the NVRA outlines how, in the case of felony convictions in Federal court, United States Attorneys “shall give written
notice” to the “chief State election official” and include several pieces
of identifying information, including not only the offender’s name but
also their “age and residence address,” “the date of entry of the judgment,” “a description of the offenses of which the offender was convicted,” and “the sentence imposed by the court.” 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(g)(1)–(2). These details protect against inadvertent removal
of the wrong individual. The NVRA also requires the provision of all
“such additional information as the United States attorney may have
concerning the offender and the offense of which the offender was
convicted” upon request of the election official. Id. § 20507(g)(3).

12

data-matching of l ong lists of suspected noncitizens  with
rolls containing many thousands of voters. Th ese efforts
are much less targeted , and the volume of potential ly
affected voters makes the risk of erroneous removal much
greater. See infra note 5. Moreover, there was no complete, up-to-date, and reliable source of citizenship data at
the time of the NVRA’s enactment to facilitate targeted
removals—nor is there such a resource today. The F ederal Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements
(“SAVE”) program, which is often  used for systematic
list-maintenance efforts, is notoriously unreliable .3 The
Federal government itself recognizes that the SAVE program does not provide reliable and current citizenship
data.4
The persistent problem of stale and outdated data presents a significant obstacle  for citizenship-based removals, especially when  compared to, for example , removals
based on death . A notice of death from a State vital -
records agency at any  point in time  indicates a final and
conclusive change in circumstance , providing enough
information for election officials to remove a registrant
from the rolls. A notice of noncitizenship at a single point
in time, however, often does not accurately reflect a registrant’s current citizenship status, as many noncitizens
later become naturalized United States citizens —and
thus eligible voters—but do not have reason to update the

3  See, e.g., Jasleen Singh & Spencer Reynolds, Homeland Security’s “SAVE” Program Exacerbates Risks to Voters, Brennan Ctr.
for Just. (July 21, 2025), https://bit.ly/4k7azRu.
4  See, e.g., Privacy Impact Assessment for the Systematic Alien
Verification for Entitlements “SAVE” Program, U.S. Dep’t of Homeland Sec. 19 (Oct. 31, 2025), https://bit.ly/3U5SCZ8 (warning that
SAVE program “may share inaccurate information with registered
agencies” and “may produce inaccurate results”).

13

citizenship records that States often use to conduct voterlist maintenance . P ut plainly, there was and still is no
reliable and accurate way to systematically remove
alleged noncitizens from voter rolls , underscoring the
continuing importance of the 90 -Day Quiet Period’s
prophylactic function.
Despite the NVRA’s clear statutory text, carefully
enumerated exceptions, and obvious purposes, Petitioner
still claims that purging voter rolls to remove alleged
noncitizens is somehow an implied  exception to the 90-
Day Quiet Period. See Pet’r Br. 44–46. Petitioner argues,
without textual support, that the NVRA’s limitations on
removing “ineligible voters” do not apply to noncitizens
because “[a] noncitizen was never an ‘eligible voter’ in the
first place.” Id.  at 45. This strained reading is meritless .
Congress intended “ineligible voters” to simply and
plainly refer to individuals who are presently ineligible to
vote—including, but not limited to, noncitizens. Th is
Court should reject an  interpretation of the NVRA that
contravenes both the statute’s plain text,  see Hartford
Underwriters Ins. Co. v. Union Planters Bank, N.A., 530
U.S. 1, 6 (2000) (“[W]e begin with the understanding that
Congress says in a statute what it means and means in a
statute what it says there.”  (citation modified) ), and its
plain purposes, see supra pp. 7–10.
To be clear, Amici do not suggest an interpretation of
the NVRA that somehow authorizes or encourages the
registration of non -excepted categories of ineligible voters. As noted above, the NVRA clearly authorizes States
to systematically remove such voters from registration
lists at any time other  than the 90 -Day Quiet  Period.
Supra pp. 9–10. That is the balance Congress chose to
strike. And there is no exception—implied or otherwise—

14

that allows Arizona to treat alleged noncitizens differently
than these other ineligible voters.
In sum, Congress recognized that the inevitably errorprone nature of systematic list maintenance required a
strong and broad counterbalance to protect voters from
accidental disenfranchisement. Outside the 90 -Day Quiet
Period, Congress determined that aff ected individuals
would likely still have time to correct any mistakes in their
voter-registration statuses. But Congress chose to
include the important 90 -day safeguard  to prevent the
likely disenfranchisement of eligible voters due to administrative error . Arizona’s reliance on programs using
flawed data (including SAVE data) to engage in systematic list maintenance even during the 90-Day Quiet Period
creates precisely the administrative and practical
concerns that NASS highlighted and Congress sought to
prevent.5

5  Recent events in Utah confirm the wisdom of Congress’s
choices. Beginning in April 2025, the State undertook “a comprehensive citizenship review of Utah’s voter registration rolls” that
“involved cross-referencing more than 2 million records against the
Driver License Division and/or [SAVE] program for citizenship verification.” Citizenship Full Summary , Off. of Lieutenant Governor
(May 27, 2026),  https://bit.ly/4zNeM1A. The State ultimately “confirmed that 99.72% of Utah’s registered voters are verifiably U.S.
citizens,” finding just “27 confirmed noncitizens” and “25 … probable
noncitizens.” Id. But the State also identified “5,007 registrants
whose citizenship status [it was] unable to confirm, many of whom
registered to vote years before driver license or Social Security numbers were required,” id. —meaning significantly more voters than
confirmed o r probable noncitizens would be swept up in a less -
discriminate dragnet of merely alleged noncitizens. See Nick Corasaniti, From 16,000 to 185 to Zero: Trump’s Claims of Illegal Voting in
Nevada Fizzle. , N.Y. Times (Sept. 24, 2026), https://bit.ly/488S33S
(detailing results of Nevada’s investigation of alleged noncitizen
voters).

15

B. The NVRA does not allow Arizona to impose a DPOC
requirement for voters to register for Federal
elections.
Congress’s balance between increasing opportunities
for eligible voters and ensuring election integrity is further manifested in 52 U.S.C. §§ 20505 and 20508, which
foreclose the additional burden of Arizona’s challenged
DPOC requirement.
Congress drafted the mail -registration provision of
the NVRA to promote uniformity. NASS’s “Barriers to
Voting” report—one of the key documents that informed
the drafting of the NVRA —explained that “[t]he
depressed level of voter turnout in the United States is
directly attributable to the haphazard systems of requirements for citizens to register to vote in the 50 states” and
thus emphasized the need “to provide a comprehensive,
uniformly accessible voter registration program for the
nation.” NVRA Hearing, supra, at 55 (citation modified).
To that end, the NVRA established a universal
Federal form and further allows State s to “ develop and
use [ ] mail voter registration form[s] that meet[ ] all of the
criteria” established for the Federal form.  52 U.S.C.
§ 20505(a)(2) ; see id. § 20508(b) . These forms must be
“available for distribution through governmental and private entities, with particular emphasis on making them
available for organized voter registration programs ,” id.
§ 20505(b) (emphasis added)— reflecting Congress’s
objective of facilitating largescale voter -registration
drives nationwide and promot ing greater civic participation. The mail registrations forms were envisioned to be a
simple mechanism for voter registration that could easily
be mailed back without an envelope. In fact,  members of
Congress regularly referred to the Federal form as “postcard registration” because the goal was to “make registering to vote as easy as mailing a postcard.” 139 Cong.

16

Rec. 2436 (1993) (Representative Martin Frost explaining
that “[his] own State of Texas has utilized mail -in, postcard registration for 21 years,” a “form of voter registration [that] has been highly successful”); see id. at 2446
(Representative Swift explaining that NVRA “provide[s]
postcard registration, which is particularly useful to [ ] disabled” individuals who might not have driver’s licenses
and “is a technique which is currently used by 28 States”).
Any additional registration hurdles beyond what
Congress contemplated, including DPOC requirements,
thwart the NVRA’s objective of making voter registration
uniform and accessible.  Federal and derivative State
mail-registration forms “may require only such” information “as is necessary to enable the appropriate State
election official to assess the eligibility of the applicant
and to administer voter registration and other parts of the
election process” and “may not include any requirement
for notarization or other formal authentication.” Id.
§ 20508(b)(1), (3). This reflects a nother careful balance
struck by Congress when crafting the NVRA : States
should have the information “necessary” to assess eligibility and administer elections but, to keep voter registration
easy and accessible, should require “ only” what is necessary and not more. Indeed, the NASS report specifically
recognized and recommended against other  burdensome
voter-registration obstacles: notarization and witness
requirements. See NVRA Hearing, supra, at 65 (recommending “[n]o witness requirement” and that “[c]ompleted registration forms do not need to be notarized or
witnessed,” explaining that this would “remove[  ] an
enormously inconvenient and archaic burden from the
registrant”).
Notably, Congress grappled with the DPOC issue  in
1993 when evaluating burdens on registration. Conferees

17

tasked with reconciling differences in the House and Senate versions of the NVRA made a conscious choice to
delete a provision that would have explicitly authorized
States to require DPOC for voter registration. The Senate had proposed an amendment that would specifically
“[p]rovide[ ] that nothing in [the NVRA] shall prevent a
State from requiring presentation of documentation relating to citizenship of an applicant for voter registration.”
H.R. Conf. Rep. No. 103 -66, at 23 (1993). The conference
committee, however, “agree[d] with the House bill and
d[id] not include this provision from the Senate amendment” because it was “not necessary or consistent with
the purposes of ” the NVRA and there was “concern that
it could be interpreted by States to permit registration
requirements that could effectively eliminate, or seriously
interfere with, the mail registration program of the Act.
It could also adversely affect the administration of the
other registration programs as well.” Id.
Instead, Congress relied on the NVRA’s attestation
requirements, which were “sufficient to deter fraudulent
registrations.” H.R. Rep. No. 103-9, at 114; see Arizona v.
Inter Tribal Council of Ariz., Inc. , 570 U.S. 1, 4–5 (2013)
(“The Federal Form … does not require documentary
evidence of citizenship; rather, it requires only that an
applicant aver, under penalty of perjury, that he is a citizen.”). This ultimate determination  reflected Congress’s
established custom: “Congress has historically relied on
an attestation requirement ‘under penalty of perjury’ as a
gate-keeping requirement for access to a wide variety of
important federal benefits.” Fish v. Kobach, 840 F.3d 710,
737 (10th Cir. 2016) (listing examples of other F ederal
statutes that rel y on attestations under penalty of perjury).

18

Any departure from Congress’s intentionally limited
requirements is inconsistent with the NVRA’s explicit
description of what the Federal form and derivative State
forms must include —and what they cannot. Allowing
Arizona to impose a DPOC requirement to register for
Federal elections with a State mail form would impose a
considerable burden in practice that would not merely
undermine the NVRA’s purpose ( by making it unnecessarily difficult to register to vote ) but also violate the
statute’s clear instructions for what registration forms
must and must not include for Federal elections.

The members of Congress who drafted and supported
the NVRA worked diligently with their staffs and other
stakeholders to create a comprehensive bill that would
increase voter registration while safeguarding election
integrity. As Representative Pelosi noted while speaking
on the House floor in support of the NVRA in 1993, this
landmark legislation was intended to “strengthen the
voice of our citizens and help rejuvenate our system of
representative democracy.” 139 Con g. Rec. 2438 (1993)
(citation modified). Amici are proud of the NVRA’s
successes, including bringing about a significant increase
in the registration of eligible voters and enhancing civic
engagement and participation.6
Though future Congresses might choose to pursue
voting legislation that balances the NVRA’s priorities differently, any such change must be the result of legislative
